refs: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 86, stomach and duodenum

steps.say: Most ulcers come from two culprits acting together or alone, namely H pylori infection and NSAID use. Eradication with fourteen days of bismuth quadruple or clarithromycin triple therapy prevents recurrence and rebleeding. Test and treat every ulcer patient, and stop the NSAID or switch to a COX-2 selective agent with cover.
steps.tx: **Helicobacter pylori** and **NSAIDs** cause most duodenal and gastric ulcers, and **eradication** with bismuth quadruple or clarithromycin triple therapy for **14** days prevents recurrence and rebleeding. Urea breath or stool antigen testing confirms cure after therapy, and NSAID ulcers need drug withdrawal plus proton pump cover. Failed eradication invites clarithromycin resistance testing and levofloxacin-based rescue before the ulcer returns with bleeding or perforation.

vis.alt: Diagram of H pylori colonising gastric epithelium and progressing to chronic gastritis, ulcer, gastric cancer or MALT lymphoma.
vis.caption: H pylori outcomes from gastritis to ulcer and cancer. Image: StewardMD.

steps.say: Forrest grading of the ulcer base at endoscopy predicts who will rebleed. Spurting and oozing lesions carry the highest risk and need clips plus heat together, followed by a high dose intravenous proton pump infusion. Never rely on a single modality for these high risk stigmata.
steps.tx: **Forrest Ia** spurting and **Ib** oozing ulcers carry the highest rebleed risk and need **combination endoscopic therapy** with clips plus thermal coagulation followed by high-dose intravenous proton pump infusion. Adherent clot gets vigorous irrigation and treated vessel underneath, while a clean base needs only oral acid suppression. Second-look endoscopy is selective, reserved for shock, large ulcers or failed primary haemostasis rather than routine use.

steps.say: When the endoscopist cannot stop the bleeding, radiology usually can. Catheter embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery controls most duodenal bleeders without opening the abdomen. Surgery with oversewing and vagotomy is now the backup for unstable or recurrent cases, not the first move.
steps.tx: Failed endoscopic control of ulcer bleeding goes to catheter **embolisation** of the **gastroduodenal artery** first, with **oversewing** plus truncal vagotomy and pyloroplasty reserved for unstable or recurrent bleeders. Coils or gel foam target the bleeding point while preserving collateral flow, and rebleed after embolisation still leaves surgery available. Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery, so this radiology-first sequence matches the anatomy of the commonest catastrophic bleed.

vis.alt: Bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer eroding into the gastroduodenal artery with arterial spurting and intraluminal blood pooling.
vis.caption: Posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery. Image: StewardMD.

steps.say: A small fresh perforation in a stable patient suits a keyhole patch, not a resection. Laparoscopic Graham omental patch with thorough lavage closes defects under one centimetre presenting inside twenty four hours. Add postoperative eradication so the same ulcer does not perforate again.
steps.tx: Perforated duodenal ulcer under **1 cm** with presentation inside **24** hours and no prior ulcer history suits laparoscopic **Graham patch** repair with lavage and postoperative eradication. The live omental tongue plugs the defect and brings blood supply, while four-quadrant lavage clears contamination. Delayed presentation, large defects or malignant appearance break these rules and push the decision toward resection rather than patching.

steps.say: Giant and malignant looking ulcers must come out rather than be patched. Ulcers over two centimetres, recurrent perforations and suspicious edges need distal gastrectomy with Billroth two or Roux-en-Y reconstruction. Patching cancer only delays the curative operation.
steps.tx: Giant ulcers over **2 cm**, malignant-looking or recurrent perforations need **distal gastrectomy** with **Billroth II** or **Roux-en-Y** reconstruction rather than patching. Resection removes the diseased antrum, allows nodal sampling and ends acid drive with antrectomy physiology. Billroth II suits duodenal stump difficulty while Roux-en-Y best prevents bile reflux gastritis, chosen by anatomy and surgeon experience.

steps.say: Chronic outlet block from old ulcer disease declares itself with the splash and the classic salt losing alkalosis. Two to four weeks of nasogastric rest with acid suppression lets oedema settle before gastrojejunostomy. Operating through acute inflammation guarantees a leak, so patience here is the operation.
steps.tx: **Gastric outlet obstruction** from chronic ulcer disease shows **succussion splash**, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and needs **2** to **4** weeks of nasogastric decompression and acid suppression before **gastrojejunostomy**. Saline with potassium corrects the alkalosis while the stomach rests, and endoscopy with biopsy excludes antral cancer mimicking benign stenosis. Drainage surgery follows only after inflammation settles and nutrition improves.

vis.alt: Ulcer formation by H pylori and NSAIDs above a gastric parietal cell showing histamine, gastrin and acetylcholine drive with proton pump inhibitor blockade.
vis.caption: Ulcer mechanisms and parietal cell acid blockade. Image: StewardMD.

steps.say: The Johnson scheme reads the ulcer position to predict acid behaviour. Lesser curvature type one has normal acid, combined gastric and duodenal type two runs high acid, and prepyloric type three behaves exactly like duodenal disease. Match the operation to the acid pattern, not just the hole.
steps.tx: Type I gastric ulcers sit on the **lesser curvature** with normal acid, type **II** combine gastric with duodenal ulcer and high acid, and type **III** **prepyloric** ulcers behave like duodenal disease. Type I needs ulcer excision with highly selective vagotomy or antrectomy by recurrence risk, type II needs acid reduction for both ulcers, and type III follows duodenal ulcer rules. Position plus acid output together decide between local and resective surgery.

steps.say: Every gastric ulcer is guilty until biopsies prove otherwise. Take multiple edge biopsies at first endoscopy and repeat the scope at eight to twelve weeks to prove healing, because five percent of innocent looking ulcers hide cancer. Non healing at three months means resection.
steps.tx: Every gastric ulcer needs multiple **edge biopsies** to exclude cancer, with **repeat endoscopy** at **8** to **12** weeks proving healing, because **5** percent of benign-looking ulcers harbour malignancy. Biopsy the heaped edge in four quadrants plus the base, map the ulcer size photographically and stop NSAIDs during surveillance. Failure to heal, growth or suspicious histology converts surveillance into oncologic resection without further delay.
